messages.content: Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.
Explain in exactly three sentences why floating-point addition is not associative.

samples.text: Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, the rounding can occur after the first two operands are summed, producing a slightly different intermediate value than if you first sum the other two operands. Because those intermediate rounded values differ, the final rounded sum can change, making (a + b) + c generally unequal to a + (b + c).

Floating-point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, the rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate sum, causing a different rounding error than if you first add the other two numbers. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce distinct floating‑point results, showing that addition is not associative in floating‑point arithmetic.

When you add three numbers, the rounding can occur after the first two operands or after the second two, and the intermediate rounded value may differ, causing the final rounded sum to change. Consequently, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different floating‑point results, showing that addition is not associative in floating‑point arithmetic.

Floating‑point numbers have a finite precision, so each operation rounds the exact real result to the nearest representable value. When you add three numbers, rounding after the first addition can change the magnitude of the intermediate result, which in turn affects how the second addition is rounded. Consequently, \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) can produce different rounded results, breaking associativity.
